content: Cefdinir is a third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic approved by the FDA for the treatment of community-acquired pneumonia, acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis, acute maxillary sinusitis, pharyngitis/tonsillitis, and uncomplicated skin and skin structure infections in adults and adolescents. In children, it is approved for acute bacterial otitis media, pharyngitis/tonsillitis, and uncomplicated skin and skin structure infections. Common adverse reactions include abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, and Candida vaginitis. Adult Dosage FDA-Labeled Indications: 300 mg every 12 hours for 10 days. 300 mg every 12 hours for 5–10 days or 600 mg every 24 hours for 10 days. For patients on hemodialysis: Hemodialysis removes cefdinir from the body. The recommended initial dose is 300 mg or 7 mg/kg every other day. At the end of each hemodialysis session, 300 mg (or 7 mg/kg) should be administered, followed by subsequent doses every other day. Off-Label Use: Limited information is available regarding off-label guideline-supported or non-guideline-supported use of cefdinir in adults. Pediatric Dosage FDA-Labeled Indications: 14 mg/kg/day orally in 1 or 2 divided doses for 5–7 days (ages 6–12 years with mild to moderate illness) or for 7 days (ages 2–5 years with mild to moderate illness) or for 10 days (younger than 2 years or severe illness). Maximum dose: 600 mg/day. 7 mg/kg orally every 12 hours for 5–10 days or 14 mg/kg orally every 24 hours for 10 days. Off-Label Use: Limited information is available regarding off-label guideline-supported or non-guideline-supported use of cefdinir in pediatric patients. Contraindications Cefdinir is contraindicated in patients with known allergies to cephalosporin antibiotics. Warnings Hypersensitivity Reactions: Before initiating therapy, assess for previous hypersensitivity reactions to cefdinir, other cephalosporins, penicillins, or other drugs. Cross-hypersensitivity among β-lactam antibiotics has been documented and may occur in up to 10% of patients with a history of penicillin allergy. If an allergic reaction occurs, discontinue cefdinir immediately. Severe hypersensitivity reactions may require treatment with epinephrine, oxygen, intravenous fluids, antihistamines, corticosteroids, pressor amines, and airway management as clinically indicated. Clostridium difficile-Associated Diarrhea (CDAD): CDAD has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including cefdinir, and may range from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, ongoing antibiotic use not directed against C. difficile may need to be discontinued. Appropriate fluid and electrolyte management, protein supplementation, antibiotic treatment of C. difficile, and surgical evaluation should be instituted as clinically indicated. Precautions General: Prescribing cefdinir in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. Prolonged treatment may result in the emergence and overgrowth of resistant organisms. Careful observation of the patient is essential. If superinfection occurs, appropriate alternative therapy should be administered. Renal Insufficiency: In patients with renal impairment (creatinine clearance <30 mL/min), the total daily dose of cefdinir should be reduced to avoid high and prolonged plasma concentrations. Postmarketing Experience Adverse events reported postmarketing include anaphylaxis (rarely fatal), Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, acute hepatitis, cholestasis, hepatic failure, pancytopenia, hemolytic anemia, acute renal failure, and others. Reddish stools have been reported, often in patients also receiving iron-containing products, due to the formation of a nonabsorbable complex between cefdinir and iron in the gastrointestinal tract. Drug Interactions Antacids: Concomitant administration with aluminumor magnesium-containing antacids reduces cefdinir absorption by approximately 40%. Cefdinir should be taken at least 2 hours before or after antacids. Probenecid: Probenecid inhibits renal excretion of cefdinir, leading to increased plasma levels and prolonged elimination. Iron Supplements: Iron supplements reduce cefdinir absorption. If iron supplements are required, cefdinir should be taken at least 2 hours before or after the supplement. Pharmacology Mechanism of Action: Cefdinir exerts bactericidal activity by inhibiting bacterial cell wall synthesis. It is stable in the presence of some β-lactamase enzymes, making it effective against certain penicillinand cephalosporin-resistant organisms. Pharmacokinetics: Cefdinir is not appreciably metabolized and is primarily eliminated via renal excretion. Dosage adjustments are necessary in patients with renal impairment. It does not accumulate in plasma following onceor twice-daily administration in individuals with normal renal function. Special Populations Pregnancy: Animal studies have shown no adverse effects on reproduction at doses up to 10 mg/kg/day in rabbits. However, there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Cefdinir should be used during pregnancy only if clearly needed. Nursing Mothers: Cefdinir was not detected in human breast milk following a single 600 mg dose. Pediatric Use: Safety and efficacy in neonates and infants less than 6 months of age have not been established. Geriatric Use: Efficacy is comparable between geriatric patients and younger adults. Dose adjustment is not necessary unless renal function is markedly compromised. Overdosage Acute Overdose: Signs and symptoms of overdose with β-lactam antibiotics include nausea, vomiting, epigastric distress, diarrhea, and convulsions. Hemodialysis can remove cefdinir from the body and may be useful in cases of serious toxic reactions, particularly in patients with compromised renal function. Microbiology Cefdinir is active against a range of aerobic gram-positive and gram-negative microorganisms, including Staphylococcus aureus (excluding methicillin-resistant strains), Streptococcus pneumoniae (penicillin-susceptible strains), Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis. It is inactive against Pseudomonas and Enterobacter species. Nonclinical Toxicology The carcinogenic potential of cefdinir has not been evaluated.
